- The FOMC kept the policy rate at 0–0.25 percent and began tapering asset purchases, consistent with progress on vaccinations and ongoing policy support.
- The November 2021 Beige Book indicates modest gains in overall economic activity across Federal Reserve Districts in October–November, with consumer spending improving and leisure and hospitality activity increasing. However, growth was constrained by widespread supply chain disruptions and labor shortages, and auto sales were held back by limited light-vehicle inventories.
- Credit conditions remain accommodative: the SLOOS shows banks easing standards across residential real estate (including HELOCs and jumbo), multifamily and nonfarm nonresidential CRE, and consumer credit; raising credit card limits and trimming auto loan rates. Foreign banks also eased CRE standards amid stronger CRE demand. Demand signals are mixed—firmer for consumer loans and expected C&I, softer in current C&I and autos—suggesting momentum but not uniformly strong.
- Risks persist from elevated inflation, stretched valuations and market fragilities, and pandemic-sensitive sectors, even as improved credit intermediation supports activity.

Overall assessment: cautiously optimistic, with momentum supported by easier credit and rising services activity, but tempered by persistent supply and labor constraints highlighted in the Beige Book.
